title: Why standing
hook: the Ardas is said standing: readiness and respect, like standing before a king

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas in joy, and your line: thanks in joy. What good thing did you thank for first? Today, not the words of the Ardas but the body that says them. Day six hundred forty-three.

A judge walks into a courtroom and everyone rises. A national anthem starts and a stadium full of people stands up, even the ones holding nachos. A teacher walks into some classrooms, in some countries, and thirty kids get to their feet. Standing is one of the oldest ways humans have of saying: this matters, and I'm paying attention. In the gurdwara, when it's time for the Ardas, the whole congregation stands. Hands are folded. Faces turn toward the Guru Granth Sahib. Nobody needs to be told why.
screen: `ALL RISE.` → `A STADIUM ON ITS FEET.` → `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.`

segments.voice: That's why the Ardas is so often called the standing prayer. Sikhs give a few reasons for the posture, and they fit together. The first is respect. Sikhs speak of the Guru as the true king, sacha paatshah. In the courts of Punjab's rulers, you didn't present a petition sitting down. You stood, hands joined, and made your request. The Ardas, a petition, is made the same way before the Guru Granth Sahib. The second is readiness. Someone sitting is resting. Someone standing can move. Sikh history is full of people who stood up for others, and the posture keeps that in the body: whatever is asked for in the Ardas, the one asking is ready to act on it. The third is togetherness. When everyone stands, nobody is above anyone else. The donor and the person who came for langar are on their feet side by side. Just before the Ardas begins, many congregations recite a line from Sukhmani Sahib, on ang 268. It says, in effect: You are the Master, to You is this prayer; body and soul are all Your gift. It's spoken standing, and it sets the tone: not a list of demands, but servants presenting themselves. One more thing, plainly. The posture is a custom of respect, not a test. People who can't stand, the elderly, the sick, someone with a baby asleep on their lap, join the Ardas sitting, and they're no less part of it. Standing is what the heart is doing. The legs just help when they can.
screen: `RESPECT: BEFORE THE TRUE KING.` · `READINESS: READY TO ACT.` · `TOGETHERNESS: NOBODY ABOVE.` · `ANG 268: YOU ARE THE MASTER.` · then, large: `STAND READY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand once. If you're able, get up now. Feet a little apart, weight even. If you want, fold your hands in front of your chest. Notice how standing feels different from sitting: more awake, a little more exposed, more ready. Breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing, and let that be your whole prayer for now. If you can't stand, sit up tall and let your spine do the standing. Stay there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Why standing. The Ardas is said standing, hands joined: respect before the true king, readiness to act, and everyone equal on their feet.
Your line: stand ready. Today, when someone asks for help, stand up to answer: from your chair, from the couch. Let your body say yes first. Day six hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs stand for the Ardas with hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, often after reciting 'tu thakur tum peh ardaas' from Sukhmani Sahib; those who cannot stand join seated.

trapdoor: what you thought: standing is just tradition.
what it means: standing says respect, readiness and equality, with the heart doing the real standing.
what a scholar hears: the posture mirrors presenting an arz, a petition, at a royal court; Sikh usage of sacha paatshah, the true king, makes the Guru's court the setting of every Ardas.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, Gauri M5, Ang 268 (tu thakur tum peh ardaas)
